utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Perhaps while the usher escorts the witness into the courtroom, I could give a few decisions on issues raised the day before yesterday. In respect of the decision of the Chamber when the accused should be called to testify, if the Defence would like to call him, the Rules, Mr. Ierace, do not provide for any basis for the Prosecution to request the Defence to express itself as you suggested. Therefore, your request is denied. Then in respect of documents, especially documents that are provided by the Defence in relation to the testimony of the military expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first say good afternoon to you. I'm just finishing a procedural issue and then we'll come back to you, Dr. Kuljic. In respect of the documents provided to the Defence in relation to the testimony of the military expert Radinovic, the parties may refer to such documents even if no questions have been put to the witness in respect of these documents. The Chamber makes a distinction between witness statements, witnesses that have not been cross-examined by the other parties, and documents, especially if these are documents of which the authenticity is not contested by the other party. I hope, Mr. Ierace, that that clarifies the question you've raised. Then I think there was still 15 minutes left for cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Kuljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first, Dr. Kuljic, remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please take out Dr. Turner's report and your report, if you will. While you're doing that, I remind you that in your evidence yesterday you said this in relation to the topic of suicide: "In Turner's report it is mentioned that in one of the statements of one of his witnesses, what was said, that he had heard there was talk in the hospital that there was an increased number of suicides. The comment of Dr. Turner's was that he did not find an increased number of suicides but that if we consider chronic stress during this period, this could be expected. So this was his expectation." I take you to paragraph 36 of Dr. Turner's report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuljic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You haven't translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the same true for you, General Galic? Do you receive translation? Oh, it's perhaps on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now it's okay. [Interpretation] It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want Mr. Ierace to repeat what he said, or did you listen to it in English or French or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I started to listen, but then I was confused because of the English, so I would like to have the question again. And could I please have the reference to the page so I can find my bearings, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the 15 minutes can start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Paragraph 36. And I remind you of your evidence yesterday. You said: "In Turner's report it is mentioned that in one of the statements of one of his witnesses, what was said, that he had heard that there was talk in the hospital that there was an increased number of suicides. The comment of Dr. Turner's was that he did not find an increased number of suicides but that if we consider chronic stress during this period, this could be expected. So this was his expectation." I suggest to you that you have misunderstood Dr. Turner's report in this regard, and I take you in that respect to paragraph 36. About halfway through that paragraph, do you see that Dr. Turner refers firstly to "In Kosevo Hospital, a study being set up of the psychosocial aspects of war." He then refers to some --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. We're still talking about paragraph 36, because you said paragraph 36. Are we reading -- it's the middle of the page. Can you tell me -- is that by Professor Logac or is this below or above Professor Logac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please wait.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it. "There is evidence in the Kosevo Hospital," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Some of the -- I'm now reading from that paragraph. "Some of the preliminary results reported by Professor Logac showed an early fall in admission and suicide rates. This is not surprising, as it has been demonstrated that the social cohesion induced in the early stages of war against a common enemy may be associated with reduced suicide rates, as in the UK during the Second World War. However, in the face of persisting and malicious civilian assault, this state would be unlikely to continue. It is likely that it would break down either with an increase in suicide rate or with apathetic risk-taking. Indeed, she reports that since February 1994 the admission rates have increased again for all conditions, especially for reactive psychoses and stress-related disorders." You see, Dr. Kuljic, you have, I suggest to you, misunderstood both the opinion of Dr. Turner in relation to suicide rates and the material that he referred to, that is, the preliminary results by Professor Logac. Instead of reporting -- instead of Dr. Turner saying that he would expect an increase in suicide rates, he in fact said that he was not surprised by a reduction in suicide rates in the initial stages and an increase in admissions for various psychological conditions at a much later stage. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I would just need a moment. Here in the sentence that you're mentioning, it says "it is true that in February 1994 there was an increase admissions rate for all conditions especially for reactive psychoses and stress-related disorders." I don't see here any mention of suicide. Indeed, she reports, the author reports, that since February 1994 the admission rates had increased again for all conditions, especially for reactive psychosis and stress-related disorders. What I wanted to say is that I do not see a mention of suicide here. I do not see the suicide rate mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you see the reference to the name Professor Logac. Earlier you said you did. Yes or no, do you see that name in the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does it appear in this sentence: "Some of the preliminary results reported by Professor Logac showed an early fall in admission and suicide rates," followed by these words "this is not surprising." Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, we read those earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that Dr. Turner in his report - excuse me - said that he did not find an increased number of suicides but if we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. consider chronic stress during this period, this could be expected. That is a misrepresentation of what Dr. Turner says in his report on this subject, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quoting my words from yesterday? You're quoting them exactly? Or are you asking me again about the meaning?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm pointing out to you that what you said about Dr. Turner's report is not borne out by the words in the report. Do you agree with that, or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that because it wasn't decisively said that there was an increased rate of suicides. It said here that there was an increased number of disorders, of conditions. Whether these were also suicides, I have no data in relation to this, and the essence of my comment yesterday about this part was about the expectations and about what exists as a fact, which I demonstrated on one example yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, we only have a few minutes. Yesterday you told us that Dr. Turner in his report referred to one of his witnesses saying that he had heard, there was talk in the hospital that there was an increased number of suicides. And I think that might refer to a part of Dr. Turner's report where we see a passage of evidence by Mr. Ashton. You go on to say: "The comment of Dr. Turner's was that he did not find an increased number of suicides but that if we consider chronic stress during this period, this could be expected." In fact, what Dr. Turner said was that one would expect an initial fall in suicide rates but then as the war dragged on, one would expect an increase. And he referred to World War II, I think the British experience, as another example of that. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand what you're saying, but I think you don't understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave it at that. We don't have much time to pursue it. Now, did you look at the report by Robin and Chester that was left with you overnight?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at both reports that you gave me, and in respect of your observation yesterday that this was about -- this was a study where only ten men had been exposed to stress and that this was a very small number in order to draw any conclusions, I would say that this corresponds fully in terms of what I said about a small number of people questioned on the basis of which Dr. Turner drew his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I see. So you say that it was a small number but then again Dr. Turner relied on the evidence of a small number of people. Is that your response? Is that your explanation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My explanation is that in medical literature you can frequently find studies that range from small, targeted studies with a small number of questioned persons up to very large-scale studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, to be accurate on the figures, the copy I gave you yesterday did not have the tables in it, did it, just the text of the report by Robin and Chester? Is that correct? There were no tables in the report.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no tables. The only thing that was mentioned was that ten men were exposed to stress. That was mentioned in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to look quickly at a version of the report which has the tables. A copy has been provided to the Defence. When you receive a copy, please turn to page 1586.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now is to address the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, please wait. Please wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've been provided with a report, and some questions will be put to you. If there's any procedural issue you'd like to address, you may do so, but -- so could you please tell us what you'd like to address the Chamber with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a procedural issue, and this is to do with the following: If I have been giving my reports to the Prosecution earlier so they had a whole day to prepare, how come that now the Prosecution is handing me one copy which I received yesterday and now I have a different copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday we dealt with the preparation of the parties for cross-examination, examination-in-chief. You are not a party in these proceedings. You are now confronted with a study. So if you need more time, then we'll look at that. But it's not the same issue. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please turn to page 1586.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. There's just one question: Because procedural issues are going to be raised by the Defence. I know that the Prosecution wishes to have a very rapid handing-over of documents. I was just given this document now and I would like to find out when was it the Prosecution had in full so that the Defence can prepare properly for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Piletta-Zanin asked me that question before you came in and I've told him I've had it now for a matter of minutes. He repeats the question. I'll now say it formally

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is it true that you asked Mr. Ierace that question and that you've now got an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true, Mr. President. But that was not the question I wanted to ask. I was wanting to ask a question about the Serb translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different matter. You asked the same question now in court, a question on which you had already an answer. You should have proper reasons for not believing what Mr. Ierace told you in order to repeat this issue in court. Now come to your next question then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question that I asked was whether there was a Serb translation so that we could prepare. And if I understood the answer of Mr. Ierace, was that there was no time to have it done because he recently received this document. Now, what I wish to say is that what do we mean by "recently"? If it was yesterday, and they I could have had it sent yesterday. And it was now, this minute, then I would understand. The question that was asked of Mr. Ierace whether there was a Serb translation of this document. That's true. And Mr. Ierace told me that he received it recently. But what does it mean by "recently"? Because sometimes we worry about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace told you that he did not just receive it recently but a couple of minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that true, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? Did he tell you that he received it a couple of minutes ago when he answered your question out of court?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall exactly what the words were used, but I believe that was the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you should have refrained from raising this issue again and wasting time. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you at page 1586?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: According to the table, there were 11 men who had experienced combat; is that correct? Is that what the table indicates?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the same page we see that ten developed post-traumatic stress disorder; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in the same table?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Both in the table and in the text, in the bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just give me some time to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, you can just follow the same line across, under "men combat" to the second-last column. "Subjects with lifetime PTSD, 10." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the last paragraph, "combat was the most powerful predict tore of PTSD in men"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the next sentence will give you the same information, that ten combat veterans who developed PTSD participated in -- and then it goes on to set out the wars - is that correct - which particular wars?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Might that be returned. Dr. Kuljic, did you also check your figures in your report taken from the article by Kessler and associates overnight? Could you please answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you agree with the figures that I put to you yesterday as being the correct figures according to the report; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These figures are mentioned, except that the mistake didn't influence the importance. It's not on the basis of that that I drew some conclusions but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the effect of the mistake. Do you admit that you got the figures wrong as to the lifetime prevalence in the general population for men and women of PTSD and also for the lifetime prevalence for exposure to traumatic experience for men and women? Do you agree the figures were wrong?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've done a permutation of numbers. It's a technical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's my 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I could go on, but I don't seek to obviously traverse the ruling knowingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there any need to re-examine the witness, or Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but I'd also like to remind you of the situation we might be authorised to refer to the Rosner articles. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, Rosner. Yes. As I told you yesterday, a few questions would be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I suggest to do is to start with Rosner and then to continue with the issues that have arisen from the cross-examination, with your leave obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. But as I told you, limit it as far as Rosner is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: With regard to the report of Rosner and his associates, what can you tell us about the comparison made with regard to the rate of post-traumatic stress in two groups of population which were mentioned, the UNPROFOR soldiers and the civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rosner's study is about examining the rate of PTSD three years after the war, among the population of Sarajevo, the people who were living in Sarajevo. And it was determined that when you examine a sample - not a sample in hospitals, as is mentioned here but a residential sample - there's 18.6 per cent -- the PTSD is 18.6 per cent. And given other investigations --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question by Mr. Piletta-Zanin refers to two groups of population being mentioned, the UNPROFOR soldiers and the civilians in Sarajevo. I'd be grateful if he could point out where we find the reference to UNPROFOR soldiers in the abstract that was provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I did understand the question to be whether the results of the Rosner study could be compared with other studies giving data on post-traumatic stress disorder in other studies. But perhaps, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it would have been clearer if we had exactly the sources, what would be compared with what. But did I understand the question in the way you intended it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, I'll put the following question to you: In the scientific literature, did you find - and perhaps in Rosner - any useful indications for comparing the rate of PTSD, of residual PTSD with regard to two types of population, the civilian population on the one hand and the military population on the other hand. What would you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across some information that had to do with research into British UNPROFOR soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Having regard to the question asked by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it can be fairly deduced that Mr. Piletta-Zanin had in mind in putting that question some particular study or studies. It would be appropriate for that study or those studies or perhaps reference in the witness's report to be indicated so that I can be assured that this has been disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Kuljic, when you said "I came across some information that had to do with research into British UNPROFOR soldiers," what source were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have here in front of me a bundle that wasn't copied last time. I have the report here. It's by Baggaley, which discusses this study of PTSD among British soldiers, the British soldiers who were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- There's an obvious question here: Why wasn't that handed over last time? How was it that Mr. Piletta-Zanin knew that the witness had that report and hasn't disclosed it, if indeed it hasn't been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please -- it seems that you had a -- some study in mind of the prevalence of PTSD among British soldiers, UNPROFOR soldiers. Were you aware of the source just mentioned by Dr. Kuljic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Dr. Kuljic spoke to me about it. He spoke to me about a number of studies. And I think I remember that among the names in question there was also the name of Dr. Rosner. And Dr. Kuljic also told me that he was able to find comparisons in the recent literature. And it is in this sense that I allow myself to put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I hesitate to become overdramatic, but this is surely breathtaking that after the events of the last few days we discover that there is yet another report that Mr. Piletta-Zanin was aware of, that he intended to question the witness about, and did not disclose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Dr. Kuljic: When did you -- you're referring now to a -- to a study on British soldiers and PTSD. When did you discuss this with Mr. Piletta-Zanin or Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke to them about this study before this hearing commenced, since we discussed certain matters, I also mentioned that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you say that it was about British soldiers or did you say UNPROFOR soldiers or -- what did you tell? Because I hear that the study is about British military men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll tell you now. The British infantry battalion 36 months after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, would you please listen to my question. My question was whether you told Mr. Piletta-Zanin that it was UNPROFOR or British soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can understand, on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. basis of this -- well, I took them to be British UNPROFOR soldiers who were in Kosovo. I think the foreign soldiers were all members of UNPROFOR that's how I understood this matter. I'm not a military expert, but that was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you how you understood it but I'm asking you what you said to Mr. Piletta-Zanin, or did you give it to him to read so that he decided for himself what it was or -- what was your discussion? Was it about British UNPROFOR, or didn't you even discuss that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said British UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give him a copy of the abstract you have or -- I don't know whether it's an abstract, but did you give him a copy of the document you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The copy that is here -- are you referring to the one with regard to the British soldiers? I'm not sure whether he saw it. I printed it out over there, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you discussed that article with Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I discussed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. You're not allowed to ask questions in respect of that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with the article. Witness, I'll withdraw that and I'll rephrase the question. Witness, some questions were put to you yesterday about the word "strah," fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, Mr. President, I would like to place a document on the ELMO. It's just a page from the dictionary. I've already had copies made of it. Everyone should have one. I would like the witness to read out what it says under the word "terror," under the word "strah."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you read what we can see if we have a look at the word "strah," fear.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to read it from here because I can't see it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Terror: Horror, fear."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the transcript, it's important for the word "strah" to be entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to read out now something, and I would appreciate it if the English booth could be very careful because it will be a little different for the B/C/S booth. It might be a little bit more difficult to translate. I'll read out what we have here, what the definition of the word "strah" is in French. I can find the following words: "Fear, anxiety, anxiousness, horror, trance" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And further on it says "i trepet" in B/C/S, which would be in French "terror."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We have on the ELMO what appears to be a page from a Serbian dictionary. Mr. Piletta-Zanin appears to be reading from a Serbian-French dictionary, which isn't on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- I didn't look at the ELMO, as a matter of fact, but let me -- yes. There is -- at least there's something different on the ELMO than I read at this moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this page was handed out, was given to Mr. Ierace a minute ago, and I'm surprised to see him making such an objection and to see that no one says anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave him the page from the French dictionary. I gave it to Mr. Ierace and to Madam Registrar a minute ago so that everyone could take cognisance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please compare the copy you just gave to us with the copy on the ELMO and see whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One was handed out yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing Mr. Ierace asked is he said it's now supposed to be read from the ELMO a document, and you provided us with another document. So that needs some explanation, instead of surprise that Mr. Ierace raises the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's a second issue as well. Perhaps we might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we first deal with the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless it's so related that we can't deal with this. Could I perhaps receive my copy back of the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have additional copies, Mr. President, if they are needed, of the Serbian text. It was handed out yesterday. But I only have one copy of the French text. But the Prosecution has both of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber would like to be able to follow as well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the second issue, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: According to the transcript, the -- when the witness was asked to read from what appears to be the Serbian dictionary, the definition for "strah," these words appear "terror, horror, fear." Mr. President, that appears to not accurately reflect what we saw on the ELMO. We see, I think in Cyrillic, the word "strah" and then immediately afterwards in brackets the letter "N" or perhaps a different letter in Cyrillic, followed by -- as best as I can tell on my poor-quality photocopy, the English word "terror" and brackets. Now, I don't know about Serbian dictionaries, but in English dictionaries when a word appears in brackets immediately after the word to be defined, some meaning attaches to those brackets and perhaps to the -- the letter followed by the full stop. Mr. President, rather than derail this part of the re-examination, my concerns could be covered if we were to tender into evidence this piece of paper so that it is clear that "terror" does not appear in the same sense as "horror" or "fear," that is, as a Serbian word without brackets and without that letter and initial, and I could make inquiries later as to what that might indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. What the Chamber would like to hear, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you hear what I have to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's -- what it is, and again we are by -- there's a lot of confusion because there's no clarity in what's done. If you want to draw our attention to translations of certain words in another language, which would support your view and would undermine, as far as I understand the Prosecution's argument that "strah" is not the same as "terror," then what the Chamber would like to hear is the translation in both directions. And I see we have copies in front of us, so if it would be possible to have presented to the Chamber the way in which the word "strah" is translated into French - and that's what you started with - and then as far as I understand from the document that was on the ELMO but not on our desk, to see what the translation is of the word "terror" to the extent that that exists in the -- this language. So would you -- unless there's something else you'd like to tell us, would you please be clear in what you are presenting to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If one had listened to the French channel carefully - and some do so - I think we will see that I was very clear. First of all, I asked the doctor to read the words on the screen. He did so, and he read out the first two words and then I stopped him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The French channel. I was confronted with the fact that what I had on my desk was something different from what was on the screen. That was the problem. And please do -- don't -- I mean, we are not debating on -- the question in French -- the question in French was perfectly clear. The problem was that we had not that part of the dictionary on our screen. So please do it in a clear way. I didn't -- I didn't make any comment on the question. I did make a comment on the confusion that was created. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So what I said again, and I'll reread the French text that we all have in front of us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I don't want any further explanations, as that we now all have it. Of course the matter has been clarified now. Dr. Kuljic -- no. No, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In such conditions -- well, no further questions, in that case. The rights of the Defence have been violated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The word "strah," and I read it out loudly, is translated into French into "peur, crainte, angoisse, anxiete, horreur, transe". And then there are some other, I would say, translations for the word "strah" in combination with other words. Is there any of them, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you would like to draw our attention to, then I'll ask the -- someone who can read the Serbian words and see what the translation is. Is there any of them that you think of relevance, then please indicate so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, in that expression that I read out, the one that is followed by "i trepet," so that would be "strah i trepet," it's followed by the word "terreur" in French. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Yes. If you'd like to draw our attention to the other dictionary, please do it without any comment on whether it's on our desk or not. I mean, you created the confusion. I don't need your comment on the confusion afterwards taking even more time than necessary. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, in relation to the questions put to you at great length yesterday, did you understand that the report of Dr. Turner's was concerned with the question as to whether there was a climate of terror in Sarajevo, and did he demonstrate any of its aspects?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you take his report to be speaking about terror?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's leading, and I don't lightly make that objection. I think it's quite inappropriately leading, having regard to the issue that it goes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to respond, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm obliged to proceed in this manner for the simple reason that there was this long dispute that was introduced by the Prosecution about the sense that should be given to the word "terror" on the one hand and "fear" on the other. That is to say, "teror" and "strah," in the documents translated by the translation section, we can find the word "strah." I just want to clarify this matter. I don't see I can put a question without using this term. And it might appear leading, but I don't see how one could proceed differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. You may put that question to the witness even if there would be some leading element in it. It's not impermissible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, have you understood the question? Could you answer it, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll answer the question again. I think that I mentioned this yesterday. On the basis of item 3 in Dr. Turner's report, I understood that General Galic had been accused of terrorising the civilian population. I won't read everything out, to save time. And then it says that "An opinion report should be prepared about this, about how such events have an influence on the appearance of fear." In psychiatric terms, I don't see a problem because if we're discussing certain events that might cause fear to appear --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I would like to tell you is that we have a purely etymological problem. The witness used the word "strah," fear, when he was answering the question, but it's not possible to know how he was answering the question, since there are multiple meanings that are possible. So I'll ask the witness this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you used this term "strah", Doctor, how are you using it, since this is one of the questions put to you by the Prosecution? Does it mean "fear" or does it mean "terror"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness gave clear evidence on the meaning of "strah" and how the word "terror" is translated into Serbian, and there is no apparent misunderstanding on the face of the witness's last answer where he used the word "fear." That's entirely consistent with what he explained yesterday, that is, he relied on the translation he was given of that particular sentence from Dr. Turner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- if you put a question to the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please -- yesterday the witness testified on several occasions that he understood terror to be extreme fear, whereas "strah" would be "fear," and then he added a word. And so that is how he explained to us yesterday his understanding of the words. But if you'd like to ask the witness whether on the basis of a -- of multiple meanings that he comes back from what he yesterday told us, you're allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please continue with your answer, develop your answer, Doctor, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday there were certain things that I wanted to say, but I was interrupted and I've just noticed that a problem has arisen here too with regard to the understanding of the term "strah." And I wanted to say that if we have a lorry which is full of sugar and on the other hand we've got a lump of sugar, in both cases we're dealing with sugar, a large amount of sugar and a small amount of sugar. If we're talking about fear, the extreme form of fear includes this aspect, terror as an ultimate form of fear, extreme fear. As a psychiatrist I can consider this sense and not the legal or military aspect, so this is the only factor that a psychiatrist can measure. One can measure fear, or if fear is extreme, if it's at the end of the scale, then that's extreme fear, even though at the other end of the scale there is no fear. That's what I wanted to draw your attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Doctor, in respect of your experience, particularly what you've told us about yesterday, your professional experience, your professional and scientific experience, can you give us more precision on whether the circumstances of war itself would be likely to cause as being the residual post-war syndromes.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely war circumstances and many others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was an issue that I would have liked to have gone into in cross-examination but I didn't have time. There's no basis for my learned colleague to raise this issue in re-examination. It wasn't dealt with in cross-examination. I'd be happy to do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is, because the Prosecution just gave us a document on combat situations that was about an American Indian population about women and men of that group that had these type of syndromes in combat situations. Now, I was kindly given this document on this basis, and the Prosecution did ask questions of the witness, so I'm asking questions myself, whether war as such as social activity is a factor that would cause syndromes of this nature. I'm sorry, I have to ask because the Prosecution has questions themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution asked questions about the position in the way the expert witness has presented data from other reports. That was the issue dealt with and not specifically the issue you're now raising. It was, I would say, purely a matter of scientific precision that was raised. Methodology, that was it. Not the presence of post-traumatic stress disorders in relation to war. So that could not be the basis. If there's any other basis, please tell us. And if not, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll do that. The Prosecution, Mr. President, asked a number of questions on specifically the fact that Dr. Turner was able to see the development of rates in saying that in a situation of war these rates can go up or go down. First, they will go down for suicide and then they'll go up as the war progresses. Now, of course, with respect to trauma --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was also a matter raised in respect of whether Dr. Kuljic represented the view of Dr. Turner in a correct way or not. That was the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said please, then, move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish to have -- to confer with my Defence counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Doctor, since you were asked questions about methods used, could you please tell us if the permutation errors that you have done, whether they could have changed any of your conclusions, particularly with respect to the problem of the PTSD in situation of war. Do you recall the intervention of the Prosecution when they said that you have done a permutation of figures?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said earlier that this would not have influenced my findings significantly because this was meant in a sense of a difference existing between exposure to stress and of the occurrence of PTSD and particularly in relation to the first war that was mentioned, combat, that was mentioned in the Indian study, that there was a difference in sexes. And on the basis of all that, my conclusion was that there should be a research done how many people were exposed to stress and how many of these people developed a consequence of that, a condition as a consequence, because simply if somebody sees a spider, somebody will be afraid and some other person will not. So we have to be able to measure something, and the methodological question is to do with the need of having a representative sample, which would include an adequate number of men, women. Also, like we would be able to use questionnaires to find out which of the events was particularly causing fear in a number of people or perhaps using other types of questionnaires to find out how many of them had psychological consequences of that, consideration that the example yesterday to do with cars - I like that example very much - so I would compare my methodological question in a way with saying that if I decided that in Serbia I should sell a music CD of a famous Dutch musician, and after six months I was asking about report on how the sales were going of a very famous Dutch musician and what was the reception with the Serbian public, there would be two reports. One report would bring me ten listeners who liked it very much, and they would be saying, "We are having a great sale of that CD," while the other group reporting would say, "I went round the entire territory of Serbia to question people, a percentage of people, and decided that it's -- that people listening to these CD, that's how many there are of them." So that's what I'm saying. Again, about certain issues, I want to have specific things, and it would be a lot easier to discuss this if there was a specific processing of such issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In other terms, Professor - and this is my very last question - in terms of methodology, you're concluding that the report of Dr. Turner's is imperfect. And my question follows: Your conclusions, your own conclusions, would they have been modified regardless of the meaning that we can give to the words that you used and in which in Serbian mean "fear," "strah"?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking as a psychiatrist, I wouldn't change anything in the meaning of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could the witness be shown the Robin report, this one. I know that you had not read this report entirely, but I need your help for understanding the table on page 1586. It says "men," and in brackets "N 117." I take it that "N" means "number."

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: But that number is not the same as the numbers under three Ns that are in the following columns. Whey mean is that -- in the first column, for example - I am talking only about men - is more than 117. Could I take it that 117 men had more than one experienced event each? I don't know if I am ...

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, if we are speaking about the first column with numbers, this means that the number of men who had experienced such an event. And then we have the number -- and I didn't check this, but if you say that this number is higher than 117, that would mean that there are men who had experienced more than one traumatic event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, because I had to understand that. Now I would like to witness to be shown this copy of the dictionary, the one in B/C/S. Could you please put that on the ELMO, please. I will be very grateful if you can use the pointer and point to the word "strah."

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we can see the word "strah" and then in brackets, it says -- well, "N," or something like that, "terror." Do you agree with that? The pointer -- the pointer. Use the pointer, not the --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the pen because it was -- the pointer is very thick. You mean this terror? Is it this terror? Is this what you mean? "Terror, terror."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that in brackets it says "N" or something like that, because I don't know, and "terror"? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a letter which is very unclear whether that's an "N" or an "L." I cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Well, after the brackets, I would be very grateful if you can point to each of the words and read it slowly so the interpreters can translate it one by one, that one.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Horror, fear, fear and terror, to govern by fear; terror, reign of terror (particularly during the French revolution); political violence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: After the word "strah," there is another word related to "strah." Do you agree? The following word.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Fear and terror." That is between the two commas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could you do the same exercise with that word.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia, the English booth wanted to inform you about the "strah i trepet," the "fear and terror" is used for a person that everyone fears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary to do that, that exercise in that case. Okay. Now, I will read some of the words that we have in the French dictionary, this one, French-B/C/S, and I would like you to translate that to B/C/S. Okay?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From French, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Well, the interpreters can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: It's because we have the word "strah" in French, and it says -- the first one is "peur." How the interpreters translate that to English, "peur."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: "Crainte.".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Also fear, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: "Angoisse"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Anxiousness or anxiety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And I take it that -- and "anxiete," [Interpretation] it is the same thing? "Horreur"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Horror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: "Transe".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Trance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. I have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Now I'd like to ask Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'd like to find out which dictionary is this? And I'm speaking about the Serbian dictionary, Serbian-French dictionary, and whether this is a dictionary which is specialised. You're saying no? You're shaking your head. But you know what the rule of the game is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know very poorly the rules of the game, because my microphone is not working. The microphones do not know the rules of the game. Oh, it's perfect. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am going to in fact say no. I was shaking my head to say unfortunately this is not a specialised dictionary in medical terms or psychiatric terms, neither. But what I'm going to do is the following, is that the next occasion I will give to the Chamber the front page of the -- each dictionary so that we all have the references. This is something I should have done earlier, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Now, Doctor, yesterday you used after the word "strah" or "fear," I believe you used an adjective which means "extreme fear," because "strah" or "fear," as you call it, is "fear." But extreme fear is -- this is fear but then you used an expression. Could you please remind me of what you said. What I mean is that yesterday you made a distinction between fear and fear with another word that meant extreme, to denote extreme fear. Am I mistaken, or did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So yesterday I said that extreme fear can be understood as an extreme version, if we are looking at this range. And at the very end of the range, that would be extreme fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm sorry. I apologise. You used -- you used a term, a specific term. You used a concrete term, a specific term.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Extreme fear."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So you're making a distinction between "strah," "fear" only, and what you've just said - I am not very good in your language - but "strah" followed by a qualifier, so to speak, and this qualifier changes in your professional field, it changes the meaning of "fear," of "strah," that is that fear -- and there is extreme fear. These are not two terms of symptoms that are identical.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is in the quantity. So extreme fear, greatest fear, quantitatively speaking we can say there was a little fear, great fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you as a professional, when you're saying -- when you say "terror," you're using only fear or are you using the term of extreme fear? I don't know whether you're following me. But in my mind's eye, these are two different terms, in terms of psychology, these are two notions, two terms that could be different.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we say "terror," in this sense, it could be identified as being "extreme fear."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Extreme fear. Very well. You told me that I understood you correctly and you observed -- you made some observations on Dr. Turner's report. It seems to me that what Dr. Turner wanted to say in his report was that he wanted to prove that certain events produced certain effects and to give examples to support what he said, he then referred to other papers written by doctors in this field, and he then turned to some testimonies that were heard during this trial. I understood that you were reproaching this report. If I dare say, you were contesting the samples. You were saying that the samples were not representative. And one of the issues that you disagreed with was, well, how can we look at the whole of Sarajevo? Now, my question is: The events in question, the past events that were studied, they were the subject of psychological studies, couldn't they have given the same results, more or less, elsewhere? For instance, I will give you one lay example. For instance, a war, a bombing of London in 1941 produced certain effects, and you more or less could conclude that if the same events occur, they will cause more or less -- they will produce more or less the same results. So this is why I think I understood that Dr. Turner was trying to explain, starting from experiences in Sarajevo and elsewhere, that certain events as such will produce effects on the population that was subjected to such events. This methodology, as such, is it shocking to you? Is it contrary to your fundamental principles of your area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we're making comparisons, I would say that we have to take into account cultural factors. Various groups of population will experience the same thing in a different manner. If I can provide you with an example from the literature now - I don't have the reference here, but it would just be a comment of mine - a study was carried out to determine how the tragedy in New York, 9/11, influenced the situation in which refugees in America were living, and it was observed that there were differences that could be detected among them. Some, more than others, relived traumas that they had already had. I think that had to do with refugees from Bosnia, from Somalia, there were -- and other countries, I can't remember which ones. That's one matter. And the other thing that I can tell you about is that in the course of my professional experience, I have noticed that the way in which wartime experiences -- wartime events are experienced is different and it depends on whether the person in question was a soldier or a civilian. Soldiers would often say that there were no problems, that everything was fine for them. And only after having had several interviews with them, only after they had learnt to trust me, they would start talking about real problems. So there is always this issue. Psychiatry is a very complicated discipline. There are too many factors that influence everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand all that. Mr. President, shall we continue for another three minutes, or are we going to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could, with the assistance of all those around us, continue for three minutes and then have a half-an-hour break, but the tape will end in approximately six, seven minutes, so -- ten minutes, I'm informed. But if we could perhaps finish the testimony of -- Would there be any issue, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is another matter that I need to attend to, and I had arranged it to occur during the break, and it is something of some urgency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have the break now. And I would have one more question for you as well. We'll adjourn until 4.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom again. Dr. Kuljic, there will be another question from -- perhaps even more from Judge Nieto-Navia for you -- no, Judge El Mahdi. I apologise, but I seem to mix up names now and then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Doctor, I'd like to rely on your memory. Today the Defence put a question to you, and you started answering it by saying the following, and I'll quote you in English. It's on page 24: [In English] I quote: "In psychiatric terms, I don't see a problem because if you are discussing certain events that might cause fear to appear." [Interpretation] And then you weren't given the opportunity to develop this answer. The context was that of commenting on Dr. Turner's report. Do you remember this? What I'm interested in is you wanted to say what the consequences of certain events would be. That's what I think I understood when you started answering the question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I can't remember what the previous question was. I don't know whether it was today, yesterday, the day before yesterday. I don't know what the exact question was. I've had a lot of things on my mind today, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was: [In English] "Doctor, in relation to the question put to you at great length yesterday, did you understand that the report of Dr. Turner's was concerned with the question as to whether there was a climate of terror in Sarajevo, and did he demonstrate any of its aspects?" [Interpretation] Then there was an interruption, and you started answering the question by saying that, and I quote you again, [In English] "In psychiatric terms, I don't see a problem, because if you are discussing certain events that might cause fear to appear." [Interpretation] And then you didn't have the opportunity of finishing your answer. I would like to hear what you have to say about this. Is it clear, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear. Thank you for this question. I think it's important. I'll explain it in the following way: I always say that apart from the fact that we can observe a certain event, we have to observe the sort of reaction a certain event causes. For example, if I show someone a spider, if I show someone who is not afraid of spiders a spider, this can be a totally insignificant event. But if I show a spider to someone for whom I know that person is afraid of spiders, then I am intentionally making that person afraid. But what is at issue is whether I was showing this person the spider on purpose. And with regard to this entire matter, I'm being asked how we are going to distinguish between wartime Sarajevo and Sarajevo which is subject to terror, and this is why I said we would have to develop, elaborate a methodological programme in order to make a comparison with some other city where war was also being waged but a city that hadn't been subjected to terror. So we should have to -- we would have to attempt to see whether there were any differences and to determine the level of fear. When researching, you establish two groups. You have two groups, a group A and B, and the purpose of having these two groups is to see whether there are any differences, whether the same phenomenon appear in one group or in another and if not, why not, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And one last thing that I'd like to qualify: Do you make a distinction between the population as such and individuals; that is to say, isn't there a common awareness, a certain shared sensation which could be diffused among the population, or is it on the basis of individuals that you reach your conclusions, your overall conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that question is concerned, as to whether a given population can react in an identical manner, I would say that as in the case of political elections, some people will vote for one party, others for another party, everyone comes out with their own programmes and everyone perceives this in a different way. And similarly, what is characteristic of fear -- one of the things that is characteristic of fear is the fact that -- the way it is individually perceived is essential. I can give you an example from the research I have carried out. For example, people who were seriously injured were asked how serious their injuries were. They said they were average or they were light injuries, and the reverse was also the case. So the individual factor has -- influences research to a large extent. In order to obtain results about the entire population, we have to have recourse to a representative sample in order to gather the various kinds of opinions which can be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, I have a question for you as well. You said that in order to do research in the population, you would have a sample of between 1 and 5 per cent, if I read your report well, or that would be usually done.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were certain mathematical formulas, statistical formulas, which determine that number, but I mentioned that percentage in relation to discussions with a professor of statistics who would say that the World Health Organization when carrying out studies in Yugoslavia would usually use that percentage. So I said this wasn't a general rule, but I mentioned this as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What sample would you need to -- I mean, you criticised Dr. Turner for not having the right sample. What sample would he have needed if he would have done the research you think would have been the proper one, as far as the population of Sarajevo is concerned?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to carry out such a study, I think that it would be necessary to take a team of experts, not just one expert but a team of experts, and the psychiatrist should also be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking about a sample, not about how many -- not a sample of psychiatrists but how big the sample would have to be, because one of the issues you said is that the sample was not large enough and you would need large samples. That's what I asked you. So what sample -- a sample of what size would you need for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something that should be calculated on the basis of those formulas. And I said if we followed the analogy, which I heard, that would be between 1 and 5 per cent. So I wouldn't accept to do something that wasn't in accordance with proposals made by -- suggestions made by statisticians. Above all -- I'm a psychiatrist above all, and in my report I tried to present certain basic findings. We all write, but we're not all literary authors, but nevertheless we have the right to write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you say I'm a psychiatrist, but isn't a major part of your criticism to Dr. Turner of statistics rather than methodology -- methodology and statistics rather than interpretation of results?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a psychiatrist and someone who graduated in medicine at the university, there is also the subject of statistics, and methodology and statistics is something that is studied as part of my masters course. And in the course of my specialisation, there are also certain elements that provided me with knowledge that, let's say, is fundamental. But I'd been asked to discuss the subject of stress here because I have my Ph.D. in that field, so in such a case I would ask for the possibility of consultation, of consulting someone, because I'm not a specialist in this field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say I couldn't give you the approximate size you would need for a research project as I had in mind in respect of Sarajevo. It's no problem for me if you don't have it, but -- you would not be able to use such a formula so that you could say, well, it would be 1 per cent or 0.8 or 2 or 3 or ...?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A minute ago I said that there was a formula and that I heard about the 1 to 5 per cent that the World Health Organization used. If you give me some information, I'll be glad to check it. I think the same question was put to Dr. Turner and that he answered in a similar way. So I didn't think that I'd have to look for the exact number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question would be: If you're talking about traumatic events, what is the - in your experience - the number of traumatic events a human being experiences during his lifetime, at the average? Of course I do understand that some people might not or hardly ever experience a traumatic event, where others often do. What would be the average of traumatic events human beings -- and let me just say, for example, in the country where you come from?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the country I come from, a traumatic experience would include ten years of war in the vicinity, sanctions, bombing, shelling, plus individual traumas, for example, the death of a relative, if someone had a car accident, someone got divorced. For example, with regard to divorces, also cultural factors that must be taken into account. How is this experienced in various countries? For example, problems with regard to divorce are sometimes given greater weight than problems that concern children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you: Could you please repeat what I asked you. I'm wondering whether you're aware of what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the traumatic experiences of people from the country that I come from. You asked me about the traumatic experience that people there might have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did I ask for the character of such experiences, or did I ask for the number on average?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the average number because I haven't come across such a piece of information, so I started telling you what kind of traumas might be involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course that becomes quite clear from your opinion. Now, so you can't give an approximate average number. That was my last question to you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two series of questions that arise -- well, the first one from a question you -- that Judge El Mahdi put.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, I'm referring to page 39, line 9 on my computer, but I think that applies to others too. You said that in methodological terms it would have been necessary to compare Sarajevo in wartime and Sarajevo which was subjected to terror, and it would have been necessary to make comparison with other cities where war was also waged but where there was no terror, apparently. Do you remember answering this question?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question is as follows: With regard to the terms that you used, and in particular with regard to the term "wartime" and everything that might include, in terms of frustration, stress, psychological pressure, et cetera, whatever the nature of these sentiments might be, I would like you to expand on that answer, that is to say, to expand on the subject of normal conditions in wartime from the psychological point of view and with relation to a comparison made with another city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Inviting the witness to expand on a topic raised by the Bench is not an appropriate question in response to questions asked by the Bench. In making that objection, I note that this again opens the door to a large and so far untrammeled area of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness himself answered this question when it was put to him by your Trial Chamber. I must say that I didn't quite seize all the details because I'm not an expert [Realtime transcript read in error "extent"], which is apparently not the case for some others. I did not quite understand what he meant when he answered this question. So I think it would be useful if it were -- if it was clear or if it was clear for me, because I have to admit that it wasn't clear for me. If it's clear for Mr. Ierace, I'm quite happy, but it wasn't clear for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue of comparative studies appears already in the report, the necessity of that. But since Mr. Piletta-Zanin would like to have a clarification. You said that you'd need to compare a war situation with, as far as I understood, the situation in Sarajevo. You spoke about conditions of wartime that hadn't been subjected to terror, people in wartime that had not been subjected to terror. Could you please briefly explain what you exactly understand to be the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I should say that the difference should be one from a psychological point of view. A psychiatrist should try to see whether there was a difference in the fear that was felt in a city which was said to be subject to terror and in another city where although a war was being waged, it wasn't subjected to terror. And having examined these two cities, one should attempt to determine whether there was any difference in the fear and by analysing the stressful events, one should try to see what is the cause of this difference in the level of fear felt if one determines that such a difference existed. In Dr. Turner's report, I came across allegations about the irregular frequency of explosions and shooting occurring. I'm not a military expert, but I asked myself whether in the course of a war there is a certain schedule that is respected, that is to say, whether shooting occurs at a certain time and not at other times. So these are certain regularities that should be investigated in order to see whether there was fear and what the cause of fear was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's the way, how you would make a distinction between what might have been caused by terror and not by terror. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what a psychiatrist can make a distinction in understanding of the quantity of fear, and after that we would have to have military experts take things into their own hands, to say how frequent were the operations, the shooting, then how much legal experts would agree on the terminology in such issues. I believe this is a multidisciplinary problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear to me. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. For the record, on page 45, line 2, we should read "expert" and not "extent," but that's just a detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The second series of questions is the following and stems from the questions you were asked by Judge Orie, on page 41, line 20, Presiding Judge Orie observed that your criticisms of the report were in terms of methodological criticism or statistical but not in terms of results. Therefore, my question is the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please before -- let me just refer, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to what I said exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 40, 20? Should I quote, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 41, page 41, line 20.
