I will quote in English the question asked by Judge Orie: [In English] "But you say 'I'm a psychiatrist,' but isn't a major part of your criticism to Dr. Turner of statistics rather than methodology, methodology and statistics rather than interpretation of results?" End of quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I did not say that the criticism of the report were in terms of methodological criticism or statistical but not in terms of results. I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- More and less. That was the distinction I made, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't find it in the text I was quoting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Is the major part of your -- of statistics and methodology -- methodology and statistics rather than interpretation of results, that is more the major part and the lesser part and not criticism yes in this field and no in another field. That's a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. That's not what I intended to say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I quoted is clear, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question is the following, Doctor: If on the basis of methodological aspects of a work we can see that one part of this work does not correspond to what should have been done, could you tell us what logical conclusions we can draw from that in terms of the conclusions that we drew from this work which we called imperfect, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJE KULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When in relation to poor methodology and positioning the problem and the error in the work itself, then conclusions are erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Kuljic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, for answering questions of all parties and of the Bench, and I hope that -- but I promised you one thing, that if there would be a specific issue finally you would say that would need a further explanation where the questions did not give you an opportunity to explain, that I would give you an opportunity at the end of your testimony. So if there's an issue, it's not necessary to repeat what you've written or to repeat what you've said. But if you say on that question I would have loved to say this and this and I got no opportunity, then this is the moment to do it. If not, we'll relieve you from your duties as an expert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some questions I was having in my head and thinking about them, but I believe that today I managed to give some answers. As you said, many things were said. You have my report, and I still stand by my report. I would like to thank you for the questions, and I hope that I managed to shed some light on these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming. I wish you a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Dr. Kuljic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to call its next expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But first, before we do that, I would like to ask the usher to take care that the next witness will be standby when we need him, and meanwhile that we deal with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there a document tendered in respect of this witness? I didn't hear that, unless we'd need the dictionaries, but I -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just wanted to say that I have already given to Madam Registrar - I don't think she has managed to see it yet - these are the pages requested by Judge El Mahdi, and I will see whether the documents can now be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that my colleague, my co-counsel expects to get the front page of the Serb-French dictionary that we promised. I can just confirm that we will either give it today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So therefore, Mr. President, just to give you a response, these two documents can be tendered as exhibits. They can be marked and stamped, if that is useful for Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do the following: I think there are a lot of exhibits still waiting for their final version or form. I would like, including videos, this to be done by tomorrow. So tomorrow you can have all the front pages of all the dictionaries that have been discussed properly provided with exhibit numbers, and the same is true for videos still to be tendered. I'm also saying this because we might have another registrar next week, and it's an impossible task for a registrar to keep record of what is still needed. But there's one issue, I think the Chamber wanted to have certain exhibits in evidence that have been produced by Professor Vilicic. Madam Registrar, could you guide us through those.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There are four additional documents: C6, trajectories of mortar shell 120 millimetres; C7, comparison the penetration of stabiliser HM of mortar shell 120 millimetres in concrete and macadam, calculated by the method of Berezin, Gabeaud, Young and Sutterlin; C8, impact velocity of the stabiliser of mortar shell 120 millimetres for penetration LP in various targets; and C9, impact velocity VP of the stabiliser of mortar shell 120 millimetres for penetration LP and various target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The last two documents seem to have the same description, Madam Registrar. Could I just see C8 and C9, because there are some differences. In C9, the last part of the -- of the title is in red "concrete 2 centimetres over other materials," and both C8 and C9 deal with a theta 0 of 55.6 degrees. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like the opportunity to confer with Mr. Stamp, if I could, about that. Perhaps if there's any issue, could we raise it at the beginning of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although, usually objections are against evidence produced by the other party, and I'm not -- of course, if there's any issue to be raised, it may be done at the beginning of the next session. But the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand the position now, Mr. President. I'm sorry. Yes. I don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has asked -- these are C exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Produced by the expert witness of which the Chamber thinks it's important to have them in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. President. There's nothing further I wish to say about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one observation so that we are absolutely certain that we're speaking of the same exhibits. Madam Registrar, would you be kind enough to make copies for us. Thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although all these documents have been copied and distributed, perhaps it's good to have them with the relevant C numbers on it copied so that there can be no confusion whatsoever. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the next witness is brought in to give his evidence, there are some issues to do with documents that the Prosecution would seek to raise at the outset, and that witness will be taken by Mr. Mundis. With your leave, he will make those points now, as soon as we swap positions at the bar table. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will try to be as brief as possible, but there are a number of issues that I think should be raised before this witness testifies and which I believe overall will result or could result in saving time if these matters can be drawn to the Trial Chamber's attention prior to this witness testifying. There are two primary issues associated with the statement of the expert General Radinovic that I would like to briefly raise at this point: The first series of issues concerns the documents which the expert relied upon and which are attached to his statement; and second, material that is cited in the footnotes of the expert's statement and the difficulties that the Prosecution has encountered in identifying this information. Let me begin with the 131 documents which were attached and filed with the expert's statement. There's a list of these documents following page 195 of his statement, and pursuant to the Chamber's decision of 27 January 2003 it would seem that these documents, since they are attached to the expert's statement, have been admitted into evidence. A large number of these documents, Mr. President, are documents from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps or SRK documents. The Defence has not called as witnesses before you those individuals who made these documents or those individuals who stored or archived or had custody of these documents, nor has the Defence provided sufficient information for the Prosecution in order for us to make inquiries in this regard. Accordingly, the authenticity remains unestablished with implications for the weight to be attached to such documents, in particular where their contents assist the Defence case. In view of the Chamber's oral decision of March 3rd in respect of the evidence of Dr. Vilicic, an issue nevertheless remains as to whether some of these documents, these 131 documents, can properly remain in evidence. In particular, the Prosecution would contend that if there is no nexus between one or more of these documents and the contents of the expert's statement or the expert's oral testimony, the Prosecution would argue that those exhibits should be withdrawn from evidence. This, Mr. President, is a point to which we may have to return following the completion of the expert's testimony. Further, there are parts of the expert's report or statement which are not sourced. Perhaps this will occur during his oral testimony; we will have to wait and see in that respect. Although his statement has been accepted and admitted into evidence, if by the conclusion of his oral testimony there remain unsourced sections of significant content, the Prosecution will request that those unsourced sections of his statement be withdrawn from evidence. Let me turn briefly to those portions of the statement which are sourced. The Prosecution asserts that there are serious problems with respect to the method employed by this expert in citing to some of the material in his statement. For example, many of the footnotes refer rather cryptically to documents based on scant information containing little more than dates and military numerical codes, for example, footnotes 5, 30, or 38. It is impossible to tell whether these documents cited in the footnotes refer to exhibits or are references to the 131 documents that are attached. In none of the footnotes does the expert make reference to any document by exhibit number, and that includes the 131 documents which are attached to his statement. The Prosecution has spent countless hours, Mr. President, attempting to decipher some of these footnotes and the documents he refers to appear to fall into several categories, the first of those being documents that are exhibits and which are in evidence, documents which are neither exhibits nor are they attached to the expert's statement or on the list following page 195 of that report. That category, Mr. President, would include documents which were marked with Prosecution exhibit or Defence exhibit numbers prior to trial but which in fact were not tendered and have not been admitted into evidence. The third category involves references to transcripts of individuals who were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecution but who were not called as witnesses by either side. Footnotes 123 and 124, for example, make reference to Prosecution interviews of three witnesses who were on the Defence witness list but were subsequently dropped. The transcripts of these interviews by the Prosecution are not in evidence, nor are they attached to the expert's statement. The fourth category concerns references to books, many of which are published in B/C/S and which apparently do not exist in either English or French translations. And the fifth category, Mr. President, refers to notes of interviews conducted by the expert and which have been the subject of previous litigation. The Prosecution would like to make its position very clear with respect to those parts of the expert's statement that are not supported by material in evidence. If at the end of the expert's oral testimony it is clear that there are parts of his report which cite to or otherwise rely on material not in evidence, the Prosecution will again ask the Chamber to reconsider its decision to admit the statement, at least with respect to those portions of the report not supported by material that is in evidence. Turning very quickly, Mr. President, to the attached documents. A quick review of the material attached to the expert's statement, which runs to several hundred pages, reveals that the documents do not contain exhibit numbers, they are not in any chronological order or in the order that they are cited to in the footnotes. Quite simply the attached documents are not organised in any apparently coherent way that would assist the Trial Chamber in attempting to make sense of them prior to the witness's testimony. As you are aware, yesterday we faxed the Defence a list concerning approximately 26 footnotes seeking clarification. Yesterday we received an oral response indicating that the documents referred to in the fax were either Defence documents which had been disclosed to the Prosecution or conversely Prosecution documents which had been disclosed to the Defence. We were informed immediately prior to today's session that the Defence has the documents cited in the footnotes that we asked them about, they will provide them to us tomorrow with translations and annotated with the relevant footnote number. But I would suggest, Mr. President, that disclosure is not the real issue here. The issue is whether or not this expert's statement is based on facts in evidence and whether the statement is of sufficient transparency to enable the Prosecution to challenge it and ultimately for the Trial Chamber to determine if it is trustworthy. As I indicated, without some further guidance on these issues from the Chamber before this witness takes the stand, additional time may be unnecessarily consumed throughout the testimony of this witness as these issues arise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to respond, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but very, very briefly. I thought I understood that my honourable colleague said that the handover of the documents was not a problem, and I was very happy about that. Now, second issue was the coming of the following witness and his transparency. What I wanted to say without the witness being here - and this is something we can check when he comes in - he was a military expert. He's a career general. And he was an expert at the time when various commissions were working on peace negotiations in Bosnia. So he is -- really was busy on the most trustworthy level. Now, I heard what Judge Orie said or some other persons, so knowing a person like, for instance, General Radinovic, it is impossible to find everything out. What is important is that we hear what he has to say and what he will say to you. Now, let us hear him. This is to do with the orality of the sources. We know that this is very hard that -- considering that the truth is that all of these documents have been at the disposal of the Prosecution for many months and -- now, let us hear the witness and then ask the question at the end if need be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In previous decisions concerning admissibility of evidence, the Chamber has, I would say in a general sense, explained that although not everything would be accepted as an expert opinion, that much attention is paid finally to the weighing the evidence. Of course the admission of evidence, which is especially a well-developed feature of the common law systems, of course it also functions in order to -- to filter the evidence that comes to a jury. It's in this mixed system a bit different. Since it also would be almost impossible to deal with every single detail for all these documents, the Chamber has decided that the report was admitted into evidence, but that does not mean that every single part of that report is accepted as being true. And therefore, if one reads one page of events of which one could not easy accept that the expert had been present during all these events described and if there are no sources, then the requirement that the Chamber has put clearly on the table, that is, that there should be transparency in methodology and facts, might not optimally be met. We'll start hearing this witness. The Chamber does well understand that the Prosecution reserves its right at the end of the testimony to come back to certain issues and to submit further requests of parts of the evidence to be declared inadmissible. Perhaps we'd rather deal with it not on the abstract level but on the concrete level, if it -- if we are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are sitting until 7.00. Perhaps it would be better to have the break right now and that we start at ten minutes to 6.00 with the examination of the expert witness. We'll adjourn until ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort the next witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon. I take it that you are Mr. Radinovic. Mr. Radinovic, before giving testimony in this court, I first should inquire whether you do hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I then inform you that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, regardless of the fact that we've also provided your curriculum vitae with your report, I would appreciate it if you could give us information on your background very briefly.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Radovan Radinovic. I was born in 1939 on the 11th of September in Podgorica, Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radinovic, can you tell us what your educational background is and what your profession is.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I finished secondary school in Podgorica, which is my place of birth, the military academy, the engineers section in Belgrade and Karlovac; the staff academy -- the command staff academy and military school in Belgrade; and at the same time I finished -- I graduated from the University of Political Science. I obtained my masters and Ph.D. there. And I am a full professor -- I was a full professor at a high school, colleges, for strategy and for military and scientific investigations. And I had the research post of a scientific researcher in the economical institute in Belgrade, which was part of the military institute there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, you told us that you were also a full professor at the -- at a war school, at a military school. Can you tell us whether you hold a rank.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am a lieutenant colonel in -- a retired lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, since you said that you were a full professor and that you held the rank of a lieutenant general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- Can you tell me how I should address you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can address me as you like. But if you would like to know how I would like you to address me, then please call me general, because the rank of general in my system of values is more important to me than the position of a professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, at the Defence's request, you wrote a military report "The Sarajevo battlefield, 1992 to 1994." Can you tell us whether you stand by your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by my report with regard to the main conclusions and findings that I reached, but I would first of all like to draw your attention to a few matters which I think are important. First of all, a comment of a general nature: I've studied tens of thousands of pages in the course of the two years that I've spent on this subject. I've also examined over 5.000 documents, operational documents of the sides involved in the conflict. And during that time I've made notes and I wrote my report. Perhaps while this report of mine was being printed, since the normal publishing procedure was not followed, it wasn't proofread, it's possible that in some series of numbers there were mistakes and there might be problems in finding the reference of documents. Likewise, in certain expressions, formulations, there might be some errors, and I'd like you to inform me of this if you come across any. I personally found three items that I would like to have corrected. Mr. President, if I may have a look at my findings and draw your attention to where these errors occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. If, on the other hand, if you would prefer to do it in writing and to present this tomorrow to us, since I take it that we might not come across any of these mistakes, that will save time, and -- so if you could prepare that briefly in writing, then we'll consider it. Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, in your written report - you called it methodology, you mentioned the methodology - what was the basis of your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Documents form the basis of my report, the documents from the parties involved, and that means orders, combat orders, combat reports, and information from both parties involved in the Sarajevo theatre of war. And naturally I analysed a certain number of maps, and above all maps which the Prosecution gave to the Defence and which belonged to the 1st Corps of the BH army. In addition to the key documents, the documents that were the basis for my report, on the basis of a sample that I selected myself, I listened to recordings of witnesses' testimony in front of this Trial Chamber, recordings that I thought might be of interest for my report. I've studied all the transcripts of the statements. I also made a selection of my own. So the transcripts of UNMO observers, of UNPROFOR officials, members of the 1st Corps and of the BH army. And naturally I also examined the transcripts of statements made by members of the Army of Republika Srpska, partly from the main staff and partly the transcripts of members of the SRK, Sarajevo Romanija Corps. In addition to doing this, I spoke to some of those officers, to some of the brigade commanders, some of the battalion commanders, and soldiers at the front lines. I also personally visited the Sarajevo theatre of war. I went there on three occasions to carry out research. As far as I can remember, we went there together. I personally visited this area and used a method that one could call the method of observation. In addition to that, I read about 20 studies which related to this subject, written by various authors who were involved in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina in various ways. I'm thinking about General Rose, Carl Bildt and others. I heard everything that the members of the BH army, the more important ones, wrote about the Sarajevo battlefield. I'm thinking of Ajnadzic's book --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. I think that you provided detailed explanations of this in your report, but I just wanted this to be heard here. General, can you tell us why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I do understand that you wanted to have repeated the Defence has claimed again and again that they would have not sufficient time. The last four minutes, I would say we have heard a repetition of pages 5 and 6 of the report. It's really not necessary to have repeated what we have all read already. So it's up to you how to use your time, but don't be surprised if at the end you might be short of time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand that everyone is familiar with the contents of this report. But given the public nature of this trial, I wanted this to be said very briefly, to be presented very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell, why did you write this report on the -- how did it develop on the Sarajevo battlefield? Why did you call it as you did?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: For various reasons, and primarily because I'm convinced after having examined, studied, many documents that a real war was being waged in Sarajevo. It was a fully active battlefield, it had warring sides, systems of command, and all the factors that make a certain area a theatre of war. And the second reason, which is very important for me too, is that the Sarajevo battlefield, or rather, the situation in Sarajevo, was the real epicentre of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina and I think the title itself draws attention, emphasises the importance of that battlefield, that theatre of war for the entire area centre of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Before we move on to questions that have to do with the activities of the army in the Sarajevo battlefield, as you have just said, can you tell us what the character of the armies was, in terms of their doctrines, the armies that were involved in the conflict there.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The characteristics, the general character of all three armies that were fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the Sarajevo battlefield, I'm referring to the Army of Republika Srpska, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And to the Croatian Defence Council. I'm using the official names that were used for these armies. These were so-called people's armies and they belonged to the militia type of army organisation, and they had all the aspects that such a character entails. With regard to the command and combat functioning and the relation to civilians, in terms of the territorial principle of waging a war. So these armies were in a conflict which was, I would say, almost a classical civil war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that the armies in the Sarajevo theatre of war - and you mentioned the Army of Republika Srpska and you mentioned the BH army - can you tell us briefly what your position is with regard to the formation of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. When was this corps formed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo Romanija Corps was formed in May 1992. That would be the shortest answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the general document 246. I've prepared all the documents. So if it's necessary, the Defence would like to ask some questions about this document which bears this number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is provided with a full set of copies you'd like to raise with the expert witness in order to avoid that time is spent again and again on the distribution. So this is just to inform you why we get a bundle of papers rather than one document. That certainly will save time, that will assist the Defence. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, similarly for the record, the Prosecution has been provided with the bundle as well as a score card. And I'll only rise to my feet if there's a document which we haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That will certainly save a lot of time and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. It's a document issued by the command of the 4th Corps of the former JNA. It's dated 17th of May, 1992. It was sent to the 216th Mountain Brigade, which was a unit of that corps. And in that document, they -- it is stated that this corps -- the name of this corps has been changed to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and they mentioned the units that are going to form a part of that corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Radinovic, may I ask you to speak a bit slower because every word has to be translated and to be transcribed, and we wouldn't like to miss a word of you. So will you please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll be careful. So in the document under item 1, it says that "The 4th Corps is to be named the Sarajevo Romanija Corps." And they mention the units that belonged to that 4th Corps and from that date they were given new names. I don't think it's necessary for me to read this out. You can see it in the document. It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, in your report, you spoke about the structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It's figure 8 on page 44, I think, and it is Exhibit D81 in the series of documents which I provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we put this key on the ELMO so the general can see it too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what this represents, what this diagram represents.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It represents the structure of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the way it was organised. At the very top we have the corps commander. Here to the extreme left it's the chief of staff, the corps chief of staff. And we have the deputy for morale, the assistant for security, and the deputy for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we have been able to observe the diagram represented by an expert, you were present when he was testifying. Does this scheme you have here represent what Mr. Philipps presented?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I was present at the examination-in-chief of Mr. Philipps. I noticed that in the structure that he presented here, there were several serious errors, and I think it would be important to correct those errors so that such omissions aren't included in the record of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were here, can you tell us what errors are concerned.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It has to do with the position of the tactical operations group of Vogosca, it has to do with the structure of the Vogosca Brigade, and also with the structure of the mixed anti-armour artillery regiment and the structure of the engineers battalion. I have those parts at hand. I could show them to you, I could tell you about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since you have mentioned them verbally -- well, if necessary, we will check this in the scheme, in the figure. General, could you now tell us, the 1st Corps of the BH army, when was it formed? Since you told us when the SRK were formed and which units were part of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps was formed by virtue of a decision by Alija Izetbegovic, who was the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, and that also means the Supreme Commander of the BH army. It was formed on the 18th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind the witness's answer, the Defence would like to show the witness document 293, 294, 297, and 289.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The last document was 289?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you have document 293 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is that a document dated the 18th of August, 1992? Is it the decision of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic with regard to the units that are to be part of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that Alija Izetbegovic adopted this decision on the 18th of August, the decision to form the 1st Corps of the BH army and the brigades mentioned in this document were to be part of its structure. That's the 1st independent brigade -- the 1st Sarajevo independent brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's not necessary to read this out since we have translated this document but since you analysed this document, can you tell us how many brigades formed part of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: 14 brigades were in the 1st Corps. But here there are certain special brigades that you can't see, certain special units that became part of the corps. You can't -- it doesn't mention those special MUP brigade under the command of Dragan Vikic, and that was an important unit of those troops and it was under the command of the 1st Corps. There were about 1.000 or 1.500 men. They were very well armed and they had armoured vehicles, Pragas, anti-armour equipment. It was a very strong brigade and it hasn't been mentioned here. Later on, reconnaissance and sabotage brigade was formed, and the manoeuvre battalions, or rather, platoons weren't mentioned. Many special detachments of battalions, et cetera. So perhaps on the basis of this document, you might not get the right picture. You might think that the corps was not as strong as it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, as part of your explanations on the 1st Corps, could you have a look at document 297.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the following document, document 297 -- 294, 297, and 289.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on these documents and tell us what they are about.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: These three documents are decisions on organisational changes, on improving the organisation and formation of the 1st Corps. In the document that we had a look at first of all, you can see the brigades are listed and these brigades have names that come from their regions, the areas where they were formed. And then new orders were issued, or rather, decisions concerning organisational improvements, and the brigades were then called according to their purposes and characteristics. So you have motorised brigades, then mechanised brigades, mountain brigades, brigades, or rather, the corps started to look like a well-organised and structured army. All these three -- these three documents are of that nature, and I don't think it's necessary to provide special explanations of them, unless you insist on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, but, General, can you tell just me if you have document 294, 297, and 289 in front of you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have them. In document 289, 9/10/93, you can see the reconnaissance and sabotage unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you also mentioned the formation within the 1st Corps of the BH army and you also mentioned existence of manoeuvre battalions. You also mentioned special units now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would like to show the general document 292, 1850.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 289, what is the title of that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 289, we have the coat of arms of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the upper part it says "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Staff of the Supreme Command." The document is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... In our --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1 through 133.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, since this is the document that was not numbered, could you please give us -- do you know the handwritten numbers for the filings on it? I have difficulties in following you when you say --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 289. D289.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see a stamp. Is this the document which has number stamped on it, on the original, 01805139 and 0180 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we were talking about the structure of the 1st Corps of the BH army about the composition, about the brigades, and you spoke about the units. You spoke about the special units and about the manoeuvre battalion. For these reasons, I'd like to show you the document 292, 1850, and 1859. General, can you see the document before you 292?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, this document is dated 9th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And this is the Supreme Command of the BH army. With this document, what is ordered?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: This is the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: For you as a layperson, you don't think it's important. But for me as an expert, that is very important. So this is the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And on the day of the 9th of October, 1992, they order a reconnaissance and sabotage brigade. And as part of this brigade, sabotage and -- reconnaissance and sabotage, there would be the regiment of the protective company of the regional staff of defence Sarajevo, special unit Sultan Fatih, special unit Boris, special unit Fatih, special unit Kobra, special unit Ljiljan, then there would be a special unit Bida [phoen], the corps reconnaissance company, and the special unit called Drago Prazina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, can you tell us about the document 1815 -- 1850, dated 10th of third, and the 21st of June, which is document 1859. These documents, are they also documents from which you can see --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I have 1851, not 1859.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is this document dated 10th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this document. What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: In this document, the command of the 1st Motorised Brigade of the 1st Corps on the 1st of March, 1993 orders that there should be special training from which we can see that within the structure of the organisational establishment of the brigade there were certain units whose identity was very hard to identify, to establish. The command of the brigade orders the command of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Motorised Battalion to conduct a selection and to appoint five combatants to form composition of units for carrying out special training. In item 2, and this is what is particularly intriguing for me, is that the commander says that candidates for training should be between 20 and 30 years old, that they should not have children, and that they should not have any criminal proceedings pending against them. And under item 3, it say that is the training will be conducted in the premises of the former Marsal Tito Barracks in the school of war skills and that this training will last for 28 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. When you spoke of item 2 that you quoted, you said that you found it particularly intriguing. Can you tell me, why is that? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for such restrictive measures, in terms of selection, for certain specialties mostly this is to be personnel that are going to be used for special tasks. I'm almost certain these will be units, these will be personnel that are going -- were going to be trained for serious forms of sabotage and anti-terrorist activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You have before you document from the 21st of June, 1994, 1859 document.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The data that you mentioned, you said that they were manoeuvring battalions. Did you mean -- you meant this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I meant this document. But the data regarding this, I obtained through the books of the 1st Corps members. By this I mean Nedzad Ajnadzic, who was the commander of the 101st Brigade and then he was the commander of the corps, the chief of staff of the corps. He said that they had manoeuvring battalions starting from 1993, while in the documents that I had available, I managed to find this document which dates 21st of June, 1994, although I reiterate they had these battalions from much earlier. Now, this is about a special type of unit which is meant for a kind of alternative task without an area of responsibility and they are deployed according to the commander's instructions, decisions, where need arises. It could be in any area of the theatre operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, when we have this document before us, since we have it, could you please read item 3 of this document, the question of the housing for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: It says in item 3: "Croatian Kralj Tvrtko does not have at his disposal adequate accommodation and the question of the accommodation of the seat of the command of the brigade and the 1st Battalion which are accommodated in the facilities of primary school Alija Alijagic and orders for its replacement represent a problem."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. During the examination-in-chief we will come back to sections from these documents, but my question now is: Considering that you were telling us about the structure and units of the 1st Corps, could you tell us, what was the structure in the establishment of the 1st Corps of the BH army? What was this like?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the BH army was established based on the infrastructure of the regional staff of the Territorial Defence -- of the former Territorial Defence for Sarajevo, then on the basis of armed groups and a paramilitary organisation which, as far as I'm aware, that can be called as being a paramilitary party troops - that's Patriotic League - in the territory of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us, considering that you studied the documents on both sides, could you tell us how many troops were involved in the 1st Corps of the BH army and how many troops in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and later on I will ask you a question about the positions of these corpses, that is, and brigades and lower echelon units within the corps.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the strength of the opposing parties in the Sarajevo theatre, tend to vary. In various sources you will find different data. But the discrepancies in data are not such that they can contest the fact that these were caused, were organised and well-established army. The Sarajevo Romanija Corps had at the time of the -- of General Galic's tenure, between 18 and 22.000. The top strength of the corps was 22.000 troops. And as far as the data for the 1st Corps of the BH army is concerned and its strength, I obtained from the operations documents from the 1st Army Corps and from the study by Nedzad Ajnadzic, a former chief of staff of the 1st Corps, and there is no surprisingly much difference between the strength which I established to be from the documents of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and from the data about the strength that was in Nedzad Ajnadzic's study. That is, between 78.000 and 80.000 troops under arms, except that in the urban part of Sarajevo, in the narrow city centre, there were between 45 and 50.000 people under arms, including armed policemen. The rest of them were on the so-called outside fronts from Mount Igman up to Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Considering that you told us briefly about the structure of both armies in the Sarajevo theatre of war, you told us -- you gave us together with your expert report, you also gave us a map. Is this the map that you gave us together with the expert report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the map which I made. I don't mean I drew it, but I marked it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What does this map represent?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: This map represents, together with topographic symbols, and this is a topographic map 1 to 50.000, this is the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the disposition of both sides in this theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, before you show us this map, you told us that this map represents areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Of both corps.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: On the map, I only indicated or marked the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, but for most part the Sarajevo Romanija Corps area of responsibility of the 1st Corps is within that area. I did not have the exact data of the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps, so I couldn't include it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "area of responsibility," can you as a military expert tell us what is an area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: An area of responsibility is a space within which a military commander prepares, plans, and carries out combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, we will come back later to the question of responsibility of a military commander in his own area of responsibility, but now could you please point on the map and tell us whether the data --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis -- I'm making mistakes again and again. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, it would appear that the map the witness is referring to is C2, but that should perhaps be put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I will resolve the problem of the map. I will ask a few questions just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's also a large map. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General, you said that this is an operations map where data has been marked, about the organisation and the positions of the warring parties. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who made this map?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: To make a map, well, that really means two different things. Who created the data, the elements of the map, and who drew the map. It will be best if I had done it all. However, because I'm not a very good draughtsman, I did not draw the map, but this map was drawn by a draughtsman under my instructions. So all the elements for this map are mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you confirm that this is the map where you have personally according to your researches you have inputted the data?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, while you were making this map, on the basis of which documents and during your researches, what -- how did you come to the data -- or rather, what data did you use to work on this map?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: The basic data for this working map I obtained from operations documents of the warring parties, from the orders, instructions, combat reports, plans, et cetera. Apart from that, I had at my disposal also one map from the files of the SRK, of the Republika Srpska Army, and this map, I believe, belonged to the intelligence organ and dates back to 1994. I certainly have this information somewhere, and I probably would be able to give more precise information regarding this. I also had at my disposal a whole series of maps from the files of the 1st Corps. I think that was what the Prosecution handed over to the Defence and the Defence gave it to me to study. From all of these maps that I used from the files of the 1st Corps of the BH army, the most convincing map, which was the one that corresponded most to the documents that I received from both sides, is the map which I believe dates from March 1993. I'm not absolutely certain of that. The date is not on the map itself. But this is a map which was made sometime, I believe, in March 1993, on which the positions of the 1st Corps brigades are marked in that narrow, what I call it, the narrow urban part of Sarajevo. So here we have brigades that are listed with all their names, their numbers, and with their lines and positions within the city. Simply, I was drawn to believe this map and -- because they corresponded to other sources, and you know that the more sources you use to draw data from, then it is reliable. I don't know, of course, if I am right, but of course this is something that is debatable.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us briefly, what do specifically red lines represent? I can't see the map very well. But if you can tell us very briefly, what do lines represent and what is actually represented on this map?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour, with your leave. Yes, we can see the red dotted lines and the blue dotted lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not on the -- but -- if the witness would like to explain more areas of the map, then we can use a microphone that he can use also when he's standing. There is a possibility to do so. So if there's any -- for him to point at certain parts of the map, then it could be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have here a pointer which can work from where I'm sitting. I find it more comfortable like this. If I can, I can do it from my witness seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone can see it. But you, General Galic, I don't know whether it is clear enough for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I can't see it yet, so I can't say whether I can see it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see anything yet. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please use your -- I would say your flash pointer and then see whether General Galic can see it on the map. Could you please move it on the map. Can you see that, General Galic, or is it -- oh, is it to be seen on the ELMO? Let's just -- yes. On the ELMO we can see how --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see, yes, Mr. President, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So perhaps if the witness uses his, what I would say, his flash pointer, his red dot, that we then have that on the ELMO as well so that General Galic can follow it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So here we have the borders of the area of responsibility of the SRK, and there is a thicker full line, and parallelly with that you have a dotted line. Now, that is according to the working map rules that were in force during the war, and this is a sign for the borders of the area of responsibility of the corps. On the left-hand side border, you can see a semicircle, and it denotes that place which is excluded from the area of responsibility -- that location which is excluded from the area of responsibility. If the semicircle had turned outside, then it's excluded. When the semicircle is turned inwards, then it is included. According to this model, we had the left-hand side border --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, the witness is pointing at thin relatively long red lines that are for longer distances straight. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us, the semi-circles on these lines for which you said denoted the exclusion and inclusion zone, what do they represent?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these semi-circles on this borderline, these are locations which are excluded from the area of responsibility. Where this location is when the semicircle is turned towards the area is excluded. These are areas around Visoko, here on Mount Igman, then more towards the south on Mount Treskavica and so on. This is a usual symbol which denotes that this particular location, this place, this topographic location is excluded from the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us, what does a red line represent, what does a blue dotted line represent, and what does a red thinner line -- dotted line represent?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: These dotted lines, thicker lines, the blue and the red, they represent the most forward parts of the combat disposition of the parties that are confronting each other in certain parts of the front. In this case, the red line denotes the most forward positions of the SRK, and the blue line, blue dotted line, thicker dotted line, denote the positions of the 1st Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, can you tell us and can you show us on the map, what was the front line when General Galic became commander? Can you tell us first, when did he become commander? And let us then link up with this period when General Galic became a commander.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Galic then came to the post of the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the 7th of September, 1992. He was before the commander of the 30th Division in Mrkonjic, and that's where he came from, and he came to the most difficult part of the front in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the hardest post of the Republika Srpska Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'll come back later and ask you to expand about your observations and what you have to say about General Galic coming to this post, but now I'd like you to tell us what was the front like when he took over the command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: When General Galic came to the post of the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, this front which is symbolically marked by these lines, this front was a lot more chaotic than we can see this on this map. This looks quite well positioned, but it was a lot worse, and I hope we will have an opportunity to speak about it in more detail. But for this occasion, I can start from the northern part. So I am drawing a line of the front, and this is what General Galic found when he came to the post of the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Here I tried to represent with my drawing also the front dynamics from the moment when General Galic came to be the commander of the corps until the day he left. I have to admit that this front suffered relatively few consequences, considering quite a long time -- a long duration of the war. The really serious changes, significant changes, that would express somewhat heightened dynamics of the front, are in the urban area, would go from the River Zeljeznica and would go up to Otes, Dogladi, and Bare, and the front in the area of Zuc and also in the plateau. So Galic, General Galic came to this curve here, came to the corps when this curve existed here, with this area in Zuc and to the Nisici high plateau with this important curved area which was turned towards the BH territory. And then when he left - and this is the result of his tenure - so this was -- this front was straightened from the Zeljeznica river between Otes and Bare, so this was straightened, this front line was straightened, and the front line was shortened, which was an improvement of the tactical position in the Sarajevo theatre. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I rise to my feet simply because the witness for several minutes has been pointing to various locations on the map, none of which will be reflected on the record, making it virtually impossible to ascertain exactly what the witness was talking about based on the written transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour, with your leave, I would ask the general to describe for the record exactly what he was indicating, considering that he knows this map best, when he was speaking about the positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Ms. Pilipovic, the general might not be that well trained in choosing formulations that fit well into the transcript. You know how difficult that is. So we'll see how you proceed, but let's avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, on the map -- I just have a problem because I can't see the map very well. General, on the map, you explained to us about the area where there was a straightening of the line, so to speak. Can you please point to that area of the map and you can tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was entered into the record, because General Galic from the moment when he arrived --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if that is the eastern part or the western part of the front.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm showing the front line towards Otes, so this line of the front during General Galic -- when he arrived, and then the front line moved on the line between Stup and Bare.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Your Honour, the witness is showing to us the western part of the front of the Sarajevo theatre, and it is on the extreme part of the western line where it is indicated --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, what does it say here?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: This is Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So this is Ilidza Infantry Brigade indication. You told us there were other indications on the front line --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm pointing to the way it looked when General Galic came. That is, the north-western part of the front. And at the time Orlic and Zuc, two important elevations above the urban part of Sarajevo, were in the hands of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. When General Galic left, these elevations remained in the hands of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the general, the witness, is showing -- pointing to the northern part of the front, the area of Zuc.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Zuc area, all the way to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The first significant change the witness referred to, I'd like to have if possible -- I know that the rule is the Presiding Judge should be on the screen, but I'd rather have the map, as a matter of fact, as an exception to the rule of what should appear. Now I lost my image. Yes. The expert witness first pointed when he was talking about the Ilidza Infantry Brigade, where there are double confrontation lines marked on the western edge of the confrontation lines around the city of Sarajevo. And when he was talking about Orlic and Zuc, he was pointing at the north-western part of the confrontation lines where they appear as double confrontation lines. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps a suggestion: If overnight the Defence could make a photocopy of the central part of that map, it might be easier for the witness to actually mark portions of it by placing the map on the ELMO and marking those portions that he's been testifying about. Simply a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, it is a suggestion. You can follow it or not follow it. The experience is that markings on maps usually go quicker than having to describe exactly what a witness pointed at, and it even goes more quickly if markings -- some additional markings are done during breaks. But it is a suggestion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps my colleague could help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having noted the willingness to assist each other among the parties, I just looking to Mr. Mundis, to see what he could do to assist Ms. Pilipovic. It's over 7.00 now. If this would be a suitable time for a break. And if not, we'll adjourn anyhow. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just 15 seconds for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Page 61, French booth, 5.000. Page 67, August, not April. And page 72, it's brigade and not battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn. We'll not sit tomorrow in the afternoon but in the morning, same courtroom, as far as I understand, 9.00. General Radinovic, may I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and the testimony you are still about to give. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
